sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: An Equivalence of Our Distance was created during the post-COVID-19 pandemic era, a time when many people had not been able to hug, put their arms around each other, or even have their clothes touched for ten months. The experience of distance and the lack of physical contact was the starting point of the project. The artist and her team sent 100 letters to friends, family, and acquaintances, asking them to send a piece of their old clothing; an "exhausted" piece of clothing that had spent its life in the closet and was now "ready to join a larger garment." The letters were accompanied by a quote from a poem: "I am jealous, I wish I were a cloak because you have been in the embrace of a cloak." After being received by post, the clothes were registered and numbered, and the process proceeded in three parts:
Registration and photographing of the clothes.
Ripping the seams by the participants using a seam ripper (without scissors).
Re-sewing and connecting the pieces to create a 90-meter fabric.

Over the course of three weeks, people sat next to each other wearing masks and at a distance, ripping the clothes, talking, telling stories, and singing. About 110 pieces of clothing were torn apart, and the separated parts were joined together to form the pieces of a large garment. This 90-square-meter fabric eventually turned into a large "collective coat." On Friday, February 19th (1 Esfand), the prepared pieces were sewn in the workshop, and with the sound of Qashqai Karna and Naqareh, the coat was taken out of the workshop and raised in the courtyard of Rooberoo Mansion in the presence of participants and guests. Each visitor took a photo of one of the original clothes with them, to keep a part of the collective memory of the project.

sections.title: Context & Site
paragraphs: The project was carried out in a temporary workshop and presentation room of Rooberoo Mansion, a room without a fixed use, which was usually a place for dialogue and project presentation. With the closure of the theater activities at that time, Rooberoo Mansion provided a vacant space for this project. Due to its flexibility and informality, this space was suitable for executing a project revolving around physical presence, collective process, and participation of the audience. Unlike galleries, this space provided a setting where people could freely enter, stay, work, and participate. The final interactive installation of the work was also held in the courtyard of the Rooberoo Mansion Complex.

sections.title: Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: The main motivation for the project stems from the experience of distance and the lack of human contact during the COVID-19 pandemic. The project addresses the issue of "presence in absence": What takes the place of the other in their absence, and how distance can be defined through objects and collective processes. In a way, the project is an attempt to build a kind of imaginary and sensory collective through shared action, dialogue, and contact with elements that substitute the body. As written in the poem at the end of the letters: "I am jealous, I wish I were a cloak, because you have been in the embrace of a cloak." Also, the project was a response to the distance the artist herself had experienced between her participatory projects and the space of Tehran galleries. Many of the artist's ideas were not accepted in the mainstream gallery scene, and the audience's participation in shaping the artwork was problematic for galleries. From the artist's point of view, this distance, before being a choice, is the result of the dominant order of the galleries and their sales-oriented economy.

sections.title: Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: The most important obstacle was the common perception in the visual arts scene, the concern of galleries and curators about the direct participation of the audience in the work. This led the artist to collaborate with an off-stage theater space, a place where it was possible to execute projects of an installation and participatory nature. There was also a financial limitation, which was covered by volunteer work, the support of the Kalar fabric store, and small contributions from the participants.

sections.title: Fundings & Partners
paragraphs: In collaboration with Ahmad Ali Kadivar, Ahmad Jafari, Maral Eshghvari, Parastoo Sadeghi, Setareh Arashloo, and Ehsan Abdifar - Rooberoo Mansion.

Financial Sponsors: All project collaborators and the artist herself worked without receiving any fee. The large lining fabric, which was the biggest expense, was provided to the project by Kalar fabric store. Other expenses, such as the courier for collecting the clothes, the scaffolding, and the closing music, were sponsored by the help of one of the project participants, who was a wearable accessory maker. A few of their manufactured brooches were also added to the large coat's buttons, which was itself made with a combination of all the buttons from the donated clothes.

sections.title: About the Artist
paragraphs: Golrokh Nafisi ((born 1981, Isfahan) is an illustrator, puppet maker, and visual artist whose works are often influenced by the political and social events of the world around her. The direct participation of the audience in interacting with the artwork, and travel as an opportunity to create new calendars and maps, are two main axes in her artistic practice. Born in Isfahan, she holds a degree in Industrial Design from the Tehran University of Art and a degree in Fine Arts from the Rietveld Academie in the Netherlands.
Process Participation took place in three circles:

Clothing Senders: This stage was initiated with the shared feeling of distance from family and friends. Invitations were initially sent by a five-person team. Each person sent the letters to twenty people, and then ten more people were selected for more distant circles.

Public Invitation: A more general letter was printed with a Risograph Machine on lightweight paper, and it was distributed as flyers, with a traditional handout practice aiming at passerbys at Valiasr intersection.

Workshop Participants: Passersby, visitors, and those who frequented Rooberoo Mansion entered the workshop. Many of them returned every night to continue ripping the clothes. However, according to the artist, the main part of connecting people to the project was the ripping part. In the end, they participated in the coat-raising ceremony, and each visitor took home a photo of one of the clothes: a kind of participation in preserving the collective memory of the project.
